content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new way of training an MLP model that can handle missing data accurately. The proposed methods were learned on 12 different datasets using four types of imputation methods. Their method was also extended using 2 regularizers. Based on the accuracy metric, their method improves the classification performance of datasets with missing values
content.strength_and_weaknesses: Weakness: The sample size of all study datasets is small. The percentage of the missing data to be handled by this method was not stated. The categories of data type were not stated like time series data etc
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The explanations are well enough hence reproducibility can be achieved. The methodology is well explained and can be reproduced. The novelty is just so - so.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the empirical study exposes simple rudimentary theoretical knowledge that is germane to the MLP algorithms in the study. Looks more like catalog of basic information on MLP and associated techniques

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a strategy to train neural networks (MLPs) so they can handle incomplete data at test time. The idea is to simply impute the data using a nearest-neighbor strategy and train the MLP with the treated data. Authors evaluate their approach in 12 datasets
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
* Proposed method is simple
* Manuscript is relatively easy to follow

## Weaknesses
* Very limited novelty: this is yet another strategy to impute missing data, which does not really depend on the downstream model (MLP here). This is a simple nearest-neighbor strategy (as the one authors cite by  Choudhury & Pal) with some slight tweaks to the training procedure for the MLP. There is also no intuition nor theory providing a rationale on why the author's strategy is a good one;
* Ignores prior literature: Missing data is a longstanding topic in ML. Yet, the authors manage to cite only 10 references. Just a quick browse through recent NeurIPS and ICLR proceedings, we can find a variety of works in the topic:
https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2021/hash/c80bcf42c220b8f5c41f85344242f1b0-Abstract.html,
https://openreview.net/forum?id=fXHl76nO2AZ,
https://openreview.net/forum?id=J7b4BCtDm4,
https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/24f2f931f12a4d9149876a5bef93e96a-Abstract.html,
https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/42ae1544956fbe6e09242e6cd752444c-Abstract.html,
https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/4ecb679fd35dcfd0f0894c399590be1a-Abstract.html,
https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/dc36f18a9a0a776671d4879cae69b551-Abstract.html,
https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/972ededf6c4d7c1405ef53f27d961eda-Abstract.html;
* Weak results: is often just as good as mean imputation and does not compare with recent works. There are also no error bars.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is relatively easy to follow. However, quality and novelty are very limited (see comments above). There are no code nor error bars, bat directions are apparently sufficient to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the very limited novelty and technical significance, I strongly recommend rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for learning an MLP for classifying data with missing entries. The method assumes that missing entries appear only in the test phase, not in training. The method is verified on typical small-size tabular datasets and compared with simple imputation strategies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Major weaknesses:

The paper does not present a justification for the proposed procedure. Why do the authors propose two phases for training the MLP? What is the aim of each phase? I guess that the second phase could be for extending the number of data points or for creating a model robust to missing values, but this is not explained in the paper.

The information that the training set does not contain missing values appears first in section 2.3. This is not a usual assumption for missing data and I would like to read such a statement at the beginning of the paper. Anyway, this setting is a bit artificial.

The model is compared with very simple methods i.e. zero, mean 1-NN imputations. A comparison with more advanced baselines is expected. The related works (in the introduction) also contain only simple techniques. What about recent techniques?

The description in Section 2 is a bit weird. In particular, section 2.1 looks very old-fashioned. Is it important to use MLP with a single hidden layer? I would assume that everyone knows how the MLP works. 

------------------

Minor weaknesses:

The authors discuss only MCAR and MAR settings. What about MNAR?

In section 2.1 the X was boldfaced, in section 2.2 it is not boldfaced. Is it ok?

I am not sure whether the clustering procedure is applied to each class individually. If yes, then what happens when there are only a few examples in a given class?

On page 3, what does it mean "n_c x r"? Multiplication? It should be  \cdot to avoid confusion.

There are many sections with just a single sentence which is strange to me.

The quality of the figures is very low.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is not well organized. The introduction does not contain a relevant literature review. Section 2 contains a detailed description of MLP is not needed since most of the readers know it perfectly. Section 3 contains many subsections with just a single sentence which is not good from an editorial point of view.

Moreover, the authors do not clearly specify that the training set cannot contain missing values. Perhaps, this information is first provided in section 2.3.
content.summary_of_the_review: The contribution of the paper is minor. The idea behind the proposed procedure is not justified in the paper. The method is examined on simple datasets and compared with the simplest imputation strategies. Moreover, the organization of the paper and the description is quite poor. I cannot recommend the publication. The paper needs to be rewritten, explained in detail (maybe even extended) and evaluated on more challenging benchmarks.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper provides a simple and heuristic-based method to train a MultiLayer perceptron (MLP) on a complete dataset such that it can be successfully applied afterwards to a testing dataset with missing features. 
The idea of the method is simple: to deal with missing features at the testing stage, the missing data features are imputed to their Nearest Neighbors (NN-1) approximations using a set of points predefined for each class.
The contribution of the paper is an augmentation of the training dataset to include new data samples generated with the above mentioned imputation technique. 
The paper compares the proposed method (AMLP) against the classical training of MLP with no missing features and applied to testing datasets having incomplete features with simple imputation algorithms such as: zero, mean, random and 1-NN imputation methods.
Results of experiments on small standard datasets such as Iris, Glass, Seeds, Balance Monk, etc. are presented and discussed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
-	Simple and intuitive method
Weaknesses:
-	There is no theoretical result or analysis supporting the proposed method.
-	The method applies only when testing data is incomplete requiring complete training datasets with limits its application in many practical situations where training datasets are also incomplete.
-	The paper compares the proposed method only against simple and basic imputation methods. There are many other approaches in the literature to train classifiers on incomplete or complete training datasets and apply them to incomplete test datasets. See for example:
o	C. Caiafa, Z. Wang, J. Sole-Casals and Q. Zhao, "Learning from Incomplete Features by Simultaneous Training of Neural Networks and Sparse Coding," in 2021 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), Nashville, TN, USA, 2021 pp. 2621-2630.
o	Marek Smieja, Lukasz Struski, Jacek Tabor, Bartosz Zielinski, and Przemyslaw Spurek. Processing of missing data by neural networks. In NeurIPS, 2018. 
-	This paper considers only small datasets with small NNs (only 3-layer NNs). The paper would be benefited by considering also the application of the method to deeper architectures and larger datasets such as computer vision datasets (MNIST and CIFAR for example).
-	There is no explanation on why a maximum of P/2 features can be removed. Is there any theoretical explanation for such constraint? How the algorithms behaves when missing entries are more than P/2?
-	Results comparing classical training (MLP) with augmented data training (AMLP) does not consider any statistical analysis. In fact results are very similar and it is not clear if the differences are statistically significant.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clear, however important theoretical results supporting the method is missing.
Quality of the paper could be improved by introducing some theoretical results or analysis. 
Besides, comparisons with other available methods are missing.
content.summary_of_the_review:
While the method is intuitively correct, the paper lacks from some theoretical ground to justify its application. 
Also, the experimental validation is limited and more results comparing against other available methods are required for a correct evaluation of the proposed method.

content.title: CLASSIFICATION OF INCOMPLETE DATA USING AUGMENTED MLP
content.TL;DR: A new way to train a multi layer perceptron such that it can classify incomplete data properly
content.abstract: We introduce a new way to train a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to classify incomplete data. To achieve this, we train an MLP using a two-phased approach. In the first phase, we train an MLP using complete data. Before the second phase of training, we create an augmented dataset. For this, we use non-missing data, delete each feature once, and then fill it using some predefined points. After that, in the second phase, we retrain the network using the augmented dataset. The aim of this type of training is to predict the class label of an incomplete dataset. At the time of testing, when a feature vector with a missing value appears, we initially impute it using the predefined points and find the class label of the feature vector using the trained network. We compare the proposed method with an original MLP on twelve datasets using four imputation strategies. The proposed method’s performance is better compared to the originally trained MLP.
